summary:
Law, money and operations in the final fortnight do not decide elections, but they do decide whether marginal votes count and whether a list ends 27 October with a petition, a fine or a debt. Five conclusions follow from the statutes, the State Comptroller's audits and the research.

(1) Money is capped in financing units (NIS 1,835,000 each for the 26th Knesset). A list that was not a faction in the outgoing Knesset has a cap that is known only once seats are counted: the higher of 10 units (NIS 18.35m) or the faction formula applied to seats won (D12-F01). Change-bloc finance teams should budget to a pessimistic seat outcome. Donations are limited to NIS 2,800 per household in 2026, from voters only; corporate, anonymous and cash gifts are banned, and joint lists count as one recipient (D12-F02). A list that wins more than 1% without crossing the threshold receives one unit (about NIS 1.8m) (D12-F03). That gives Reservists-Economic (about 1.6%) and Amcha (about 1.3%) a money reason to stay in, while Blue and White (about 0.6%) gains nothing by staying. Enforcement is late and modest: fines of NIS 50k-1.2m, reported two years on (D12-F04). The real exposures are post-election debt and the rules on third parties and cross-list spending (D12-F05, D12-F06). Joint 'vote change' ads and allied-NGO activity need written cost allocation and arm's-length structures.

(2) The propaganda law sets a fixed calendar. Broadcasts run 13-26 Oct and give faction-based lists far more airtime (D12-F08). Propaganda by rallies, processions, loudspeakers or broadcast must stop at 19:00 on 26 Oct, and the 5-metre exclusion zone applies on the day itself (D12-F14). The poll blackout begins at the end of Friday 23 Oct, and every poll published before then needs the full disclosure block (D12-F07). Gifts, food and entertainment linked to propaganda are banned, so US-style election-day festivals are not available to parties (D12-F09). Rides to the polls are lawful but anything else of value is not (D12-F10). The 2026 CEC has already removed Yashar and Bennett material over IDF imagery and enforces new deepfake labels (D12-F12, D12-F13). Creative work needs same-day legal clearance, and a petitions desk should be ready to strike back.

(3) Data compliance is now the most likely way to get into trouble. The register may be used only for the campaign and must be deleted afterwards, together with vendors' copies (D12-F21). Since Amendment 13, fines are counted per record (D12-F22). Segmented SMS and WhatsApp messages are 'direct mail' and need notices and opt-outs (D12-F24). Brokered 'enriched' phone lists are the main hazard (D12-F23). The High Court's ban on reporting who voted (D5-F25) means election-day mobilisation must run on the CEC's aggregate station turnout releases (D5-F26) and on supporters' self-reports.

(4) Vote protection in Israel is a matter of counting accuracy, not of deterring fraud. In high-fraud countries, randomised observers cut the incumbent's share by 6-11 points (D12-F32, D12-F33), and photo checks of results sheets cut aggregation fraud (D12-F34). Israel is different. The CEC already places two neutral secretaries and camera-carrying inspectors, and in 2021 its own audit found police-grade evidence at only 10 of about 13,240 stations (D12-F16, D12-F17). Even so, corrections and annulments moved seats twice in 2019 on margins of a few hundred votes (D12-F18), and in 2022 the invalid-ballot pool was seven times Meretz's shortfall (D12-F19). Our analysis of the CEC data shows invalid rates ranging from 0.22% to 1.13% across segments, with YB's Russian-speaking base at 0.80% against 0.35% in liberal cities (D12-F20). Committee seats belong to the factions of the outgoing Knesset; lists without one get observers only, and seats a faction does not fill are lost (D12-F15). The bloc therefore needs one joint staffing map, a protocol-photo results desk and ballot-mechanics reminders.

(5) Organisation evidence favours using what already exists. Field offices add only 0.3-1 point locally (D12-F25). Volunteer leaders who own a turf (D12-F26), debrief calls (42% vs 12.5% return, D12-F27) and matching messengers to the voters they contact (D12-F28) matter more than infrastructure. Untested framing (D12-F29) and broad digital ads (D12-F31) do not move turnout, so the bloc should test what it can and fund contact.

findings.topic: Party Financing Law: state funding and spending caps
findings.claim: State election funding and the legal ceiling on election spending are both counted in 'financing units'. For the 26th Knesset a list gets one unit per seat (for an existing faction, the mean of its outgoing and new seats) plus 1.4 units under a temporary provision, and factions can draw an advance of 80% of a unit per outgoing MK. The spending cap depends on the faction's size on the determining day: 10 units for up to 5 MKs, 2 units per MK for 6-10 MKs, and 20 units plus 1.5 per MK above ten for 11+ MKs, never more than 70 units. A list that was not a faction gets the higher of 10 units or the faction formula applied to the seats it actually wins.
findings.quant: Financing unit for 26th Knesset election expenses: NIS 1,835,000 (Yalkut Pirsumim notice 7682); unit from Jan 2026 for current funding NIS 1,638,000. Our arithmetic: 10 units = NIS 18.35m; 70 units = NIS 128.45m; a 24-MK faction cap = 41 units = NIS 75.2m. For a new list the cap is known only after the count: 23 seats -> 39.5 units (NIS 72.5m), 18 seats -> 32 units (NIS 58.7m).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Party Financing Law, 5733-1973, ss. 1, 3, 4, 7 (Hebrew consolidated text)
findings.relevance: Each change-bloc list must manage spending against a cap set in units. For a list without an outgoing faction, spending above the 10-unit floor (NIS 18.35m) is a bet on seats won: a list that spends for 23 seats and wins 18 is over the cap. The finance team should cap final-fortnight spending at the cap implied by a pessimistic seat outcome (for example the forecast's 10th percentile), not the mean.

findings.topic: Donation limits and banned sources
findings.claim: Parties and lists may accept donations only from individuals who are registered voters. Donations from corporations (Israeli or foreign), anonymous donations and cash are banned, and donors' identities and addresses must be verified. In an election year each person and household may give at most an indexed NIS 1,000 (2026 value NIS 2,800) to a party. The parties of a joint list count as one faction for the election-year cap, so a household cannot give the maximum to each component. An illegal donation must be returned, and the party pays the state up to twice its value; knowingly giving or taking one is a crime (up to 1 year).
findings.quant: 2026 caps per person/household: NIS 2,800 in an election year; NIS 1,100 in other years. Sanction: repayment of up to 2x the illegal donation. Lists that waive public funding: cap NIS 150,400 (2026 value). Amounts indexed each 1 January.
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Party Financing Law, 5733-1973, ss. 8, 8c, 9a, 13b(f)
findings.relevance: Fundraising in the last two weeks is small-donor only. Together (Bennett 2026 + Yesh Atid) and The Democrats (Labor + Meretz) are joint lists, so a household's NIS 2,800 limit covers the whole list. In-kind help from companies (free venues, vehicles, software, data, printing) is a banned corporate donation and must be invoiced at market price.

findings.topic: Lists that win over 1% but miss the threshold are paid one unit
findings.claim: A list that wins more than 1% of valid votes but takes no seats is entitled to one financing unit for election expenses: 85% after the results and 15% after a positive State Comptroller report, minus any advance it drew. Lists drawing advances must post bank guarantees, and the guarantee is called if the advance exceeds what the list is finally owed. Below 1%, a list gets nothing and must repay its advance.
findings.quant: 1 unit = NIS 1.835m. Our arithmetic on 2022 valid votes (4,764,742): 1% is about 47,600 votes. Forecast: Reservists-Economic about 1.6% (about 76,000), Amcha about 1.3% (about 62,000), Blue and White about 0.6% (about 28,600).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Party Financing Law, 5733-1973, ss. 2(a1), 4(a1)-(c2), 13c
findings.relevance: This changes the rescue calculus. Reservists-Economic and Amcha each stand to receive about NIS 1.8m if they stay in and finish above 1%, so a public 'wasted vote' appeal argues against their finances. Blue and White at about 0.6% gets nothing by staying in, which is consistent with the reported withdrawal talk. Any negotiated withdrawal has to deal with debts and guarantees (our inference; not a legal opinion).

findings.topic: State Comptroller enforcement: sanctions and track record
findings.claim: The State Comptroller audits each list's election accounts, which are due 24 weeks after the results; the Comptroller then has 24 weeks to report. A non-positive report means 15% of election funding is withheld, and overspending costs one-third of the excess, capped at 20% of the entitlement. Past audits produced fines and documented large deficits. They arrived 1.5-2 years after the vote.
findings.quant: 2015 election (report Oct 2016): Likud ~NIS 850k, Jewish Home ~NIS 850k, Joint List NIS 1.2m, YB ~NIS 200k; deficits Yesh Atid NIS 16m, Likud NIS 10m, YB NIS 9m; all parties combined ~NIS 60m. Sept 2019 election (report Nov 2021): Likud, Labor, Atzmaut and Meretz NIS 200k each; Likud an extra NIS 50k for its pre-election 'Leumiada' conference. The Comptroller found signs of paid follower-boosting and fake accounts but could not attribute them to parties.
findings.authors: Times of Israel staff (reporting State Comptroller reports)
findings.title: Parties fined millions over Tel Aviv rally ahead of 2015 vote; Political parties fined over campaign finance violations during 2019 elections
findings.relevance: Sanctions are small relative to budgets and arrive late, but they are deducted from future public funding. The binding constraint is post-election debt: Yesh Atid carried the largest 2015 deficit. Party events dressed as non-election conferences (the 'Leumiada' precedent) are fined.

findings.topic: Third-party 'bodies active in elections' (2017 V15 amendment)
findings.claim: Since the 2017 amendment, groups outside the lists that spend above a threshold on election activity must register with the State Comptroller, organise as an association or public-benefit company, run a website, and publish each donation within 7 days during the election period. Donations to them are capped, foreign money may not exceed one-third, and above a higher tier they need an auditor. The covered activities include voter databases linking ID to voting intention, free transport to the polls on election day, direct appeals to vote for or against a list, and propaganda. Candidates and senior party officials may not hold senior roles in such bodies.
findings.quant: Registration threshold: NIS 100,000 indexed (NIS 120,400 in 2026). Donations published within 7 days in the election period (14 otherwise). Foreign donations at most 1/3 of the total. Passed 41-27 (Mar 2017; sponsor MK Yoav Kisch).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute); JNi.Media (passage report)
findings.title: Party Financing Law s. 10c; 'Knesset passes V-15 law to limit PACs' influence on elections'
findings.venue: Hebrew Wikisource consolidation; The Jewish Press
findings.relevance: Allied civil-society efforts (reservist and protest movements, expat Fly&Vote, independent Arab-sector GOTV, transport schemes) are regulated election actors once above about NIS 120k, and their candidate and party officials cannot run them. Cross-ref D6-F23, D5-F29. Coordination with them must stay at arm's length and be cleared by counsel.

findings.topic: Linked bodies and cross-list spending
findings.claim: Spending by bodies linked to a party counts as party spending (Party Financing Law s. 10a, as summarised by International IDEA). In the 2015 Rabin Square cases the Comptroller held that parties which actively used a rally organised by others had received a prohibited donation. He fined none of the parties at the 7 March 'Israel wants change' rally, because they had neither organised nor promoted it. Parties on a joint list must sign an election-expense agreement and may keep joint or separate accounts.
findings.quant: 2015: the 15 March right-wing rally was treated as a prohibited donation to Likud, Jewish Home, YB and Yachad; there were no fines over the 7 March centre-left rally. The overall fines in that report (Likud and JH ~NIS 850k each) covered several infractions.
findings.authors: Times of Israel staff; International IDEA (summary of s. 10a)
findings.title: Parties fined millions over Tel Aviv rally ahead of 2015 vote
findings.venue: The Times of Israel; IDEA Political Finance Database
findings.relevance: Joint 'vote change' advertising, shared field offices or joint rallies paid by one list for several lists are in-kind transfers between parties. Parties are corporate bodies and corporate donations are banned, so costs must be split in writing (our inference, to confirm with counsel). Protest-movement rallies in the final week must not turn into party events at which candidates speak with the parties' involvement.

findings.topic: Polls: disclosure rules and the blackout
findings.claim: Anyone who publishes an election survey must state who commissioned it, who conducted it, the fieldwork dates, the population sampled, how many were approached and how many took part, and the margin of error. Print and online publishers must also give the questions. Unscientific polls must be labelled as such. The pollster must send the CEC the full methods 'as soon as possible', report to the State Comptroller (including who funded the poll) within 20 days after election day, and keep the data for 3 years. From the end of the Friday before polling day until the polls close, nobody may publish new poll results, and republished older polls must be labelled 'not current'.
findings.quant: Blackout: end of Fri 23 Oct 2026 to 22:00 Tue 27 Oct 2026, so exit polls appear at 22:00. Comptroller report due within 20 days of election day (16 Nov 2026). Penalty for breach of the law: up to 6 months' imprisonment or a fine (s. 17).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, 5719-1959, ss. 16e, 17
findings.relevance: Internal polls the campaign leaks or posts during 24-27 Oct are illegal publications, including 'hinted' results on social media. Any poll released before then needs the full disclosure block. Polls a list commissions are reported to the Comptroller with their funder, so they are visible as campaign expenses.

findings.topic: Election broadcasts: airtime and timing
findings.claim: Free campaign broadcasts on TV and radio run only in the 14 days before the election and not on rest days. Each list gets 7 TV minutes and 15 radio minutes. A list submitted by a party that is a faction in the outgoing Knesset gets 2 extra TV minutes and 4 extra radio minutes per sitting MK. Outside these broadcasts, election propaganda on radio and TV is banned for the 60 days before the vote.
findings.quant: Window: 13-26 Oct 2026 (broadcast propaganda also ends at 19:00 on 26 Oct, s. 129 Knesset Elections Law). Illustration (our arithmetic): a list built on a 24-MK faction gets 7 + 48 = 55 TV minutes; a list with no outgoing faction gets 7.
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, 5719-1959, ss. 5, 15, 15a
findings.relevance: Airtime is very unequal: faction-based lists such as Yesh Atid inside Together and YB far out-broadcast a new list like Yashar if it has no outgoing faction. TV persuasion is small and decays within days (P-F04, P-F06), so the slots are best used late, for turnout and coalition-signal messages, rather than early persuasion.

findings.topic: Gifts, food, drink and entertainment
findings.claim: Election propaganda may not be tied to gifts and may not accompany entertainment, including artists' performances, music, singing, film screenings and torch processions. Propaganda may not be linked to serving food or alcohol, except at parties in private homes. The ban applies throughout the 90-day restricted period and on election day.
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, 5719-1959, ss. 2, 8
findings.relevance: The US election-day festival tactic (D3-F13: +2.6 to +6.5 pp) cannot be copied as a party event with music, performers or free food. House meetings with refreshments in private homes are the legal format for social gatherings. Election-day 'thank-you' gifts at polling places, for which Likud was criticised in 2019, are out.

findings.topic: Vote buying, benefits and the transport exception
findings.claim: Offering or giving a bribe to vote or abstain is a crime punishable by up to 5 years. So is promising a job, threatening dismissal, or using oaths, curses or amulets. A bribe includes any service or 'other benefit', given directly or through someone else, before or after the vote. The law expressly says that driving a voter to and from the polling station is not a bribe. Intercity transport on election day is state-funded through the CEC.
findings.quant: s. 122 penalty: up to 5 years or a fine. Reported precedent (2013 campaign): the CEC said a YB candidate's promise of paid polling-station jobs to the activists who brought out the most voters was illegal.
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Knesset Elections Law [Consolidated Version], 5729-1969, ss. 122, 123, 134a
findings.relevance: Rides to the polls by the lists' own volunteers are lawful, and parties have long arranged them. Anything of value beyond the ride, such as meals, paid days, lodging, flights or vouchers, is a benefit. Third parties that offer free transport must register (D12-F05). Cross-ref D6-F23 (Zazim ruling), D5-F28 (free intercity transport), D5-F29 (Fly&Vote compromise).

findings.topic: Signs, letters and loudspeakers
findings.claim: A list's ballot letters may be used in propaganda only during the 42 days before the election. Posters may be put up only on boards the local authority designates. Pasting, painting or projecting light onto buildings, fences, roads and pavements is banned, though homes and party offices may display material subject to by-laws. Billboards and bus advertising have their own rules (s. 10b). Loudspeaker propaganda is allowed only at assemblies.
findings.quant: Letter-use window opened 15 Sep 2026 (D-42).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, 5719-1959, ss. 4, 7, 9, 10, 10a, 10b
findings.relevance: Volunteer 'guerrilla' signage (stickers on poles, chalk, projections) is unlawful and invites petitions and fines. Balcony and window signs in supporters' homes are lawful and a cheap way to show visible local support in Turnout-engine neighbourhoods.

findings.topic: Public assets, the IDF and children in propaganda; 2026 rulings against change-bloc lists
findings.claim: Propaganda may not use the money or property of state-audited bodies (s. 2a). In the restricted period it may not use the IDF in a way that suggests the army is linked to a list, nor the name or image of fallen or wounded soldiers or victims of hostile action without written consent (s. 2b), nor children under 15 (s. 2c). In 2026 CEC chair Justice Noam Sohlberg granted a Likud petition and ordered Yashar to remove a video with AI-generated soldiers. He held that the public-assets ban applied even though the video was published before the IDF ban took effect. On 19 Aug 2026, on another Likud petition, he ordered Bennett (Together) to cut the segments of a campaign video showing soldiers in operational activity and an IDF artillery piece. On 17-18 Sep 2026 Likud also petitioned for the removal of three Yashar videos about Netanyahu's conduct before 7 October, calling their editing misleading; no ruling had been issued when this was reported.
findings.quant: Bennett order 19 Aug 2026, partial (only the IDF segments). Yashar AI-soldiers order: date not retrieved. Likud petition against three Yashar videos filed 18 Sep 2026 after a 10:00, 17 Sep removal ultimatum.
findings.authors: Amir Ettinger (Ynet); Hezki Baruch (Arutz Sheva); Anna Barsky (Jerusalem Post); Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Sohlberg accepts Likud's petition: orders Eisenkot to remove AI-generated video featuring soldiers; Following Likud petition: Bennett ordered to remove footage of IDF soldiers from video; Likud files petition demanding Eisenkot's Yashar remove anti-Netanyahu ads
findings.venue: Ynetnews; Israel National News; The Jerusalem Post; Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law ss. 2a-2c
findings.relevance: Yashar (a former chief of staff's list) and Together sell security credentials, so they are the lists most exposed to Likud petitions over IDF imagery. Likud is running a systematic petitions strategy against these lists. Every final-fortnight creative with uniforms, bases, weapons, the fallen or children, and every edited news clip, needs legal pre-clearance with an archived source file, because a removal order in the last week costs both the asset and the news cycle.

findings.topic: Deepfake disclosure and sponsor identification (new 2026 rules)
findings.claim: A temporary provision, s. 2a2 (in force 23 Jul 2026 to 26 Oct 2027), requires election propaganda that is a 'deep fake' (audio-visual content created or materially altered digitally, including by AI) to carry a clear and prominent disclosure. The CEC issued binding format rules on 26 Jul 2026: two standard symbols or a text notice; at least 5% of the content's height (minimum 10 pt) for print and images; on screen for the whole of a video; read at the start and end of audio. Separately, every election ad, including paid online content, must name the person responsible for commissioning it and how to contact them (s. 2a1).
findings.quant: Rules issued 26 Jul 2026; label size at least max(5% of height, 10 pt); video label on screen 100% of the duration.
findings.authors: Haim Ravia; Dotan Hammer (Pearl Cohen), summarising CEC rules
findings.title: Israel Issues Deepfake Disclosure Rules for Election Campaign Publications
findings.venue: Pearl Cohen client alert; Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law ss. 2a1, 2a2
findings.relevance: The change bloc should keep a monitoring and petition desk that can file the same day, and should make sure all its own synthetic or edited content, including volunteer-made memes paid or boosted by the list, carries the standard label and sponsor line.

findings.topic: Election-day limits around polling stations
findings.claim: On election day, propaganda of any kind is an offence inside a polling place or within 5 metres of its entrance gate; where there is no yard or fence the distance is 10 metres from the outer walls. From 19:00 on the eve of the election, propaganda by rallies, processions, loudspeakers and radio or TV broadcast is banned. Only authorised people may be present in the polling room. The election regulations bar phone conversations in the room while a voter is present and during the count, except to run the vote or in an emergency. On 17 Sep 2026 the High Court barred party representatives from passing identifiable voters' names to their parties (D5-F25).
findings.quant: Exclusion zone: 5 m from the gate (10 m from the walls without a fence); penalty up to 6 months. Eve cut-off: 19:00 Mon 26 Oct 2026. Polls open 07:00-22:00 (D2-F17).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute); Rachel Aridor Hershkovitz & Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler (on reg. 45a)
findings.title: Knesset Elections Law ss. 73, 126(5), 129; Privacy and Elections: Toward the 2026 Elections (IDI Policy Paper 64)
findings.venue: Hebrew Wikisource consolidation; Israel Democracy Institute
findings.relevance: Street teams may work outside the 5 m line, but no closer. The last mass events must end before 19:00 on 26 Oct. Committee members and observers may not phone or app-report who voted: election-day mobilisation must be driven by the CEC's aggregate station turnout releases (D5-F26) and by supporters' self-reports, not by data from inside the polling room.

findings.topic: Polling committees: who sits, deadlines, observers' rights
findings.claim: The CEC fixes each polling committee's size and faction mix no later than the 40th day before the election, with at least three factions per committee. Factions appoint their members, deputies and permanent alternates and may replace them at any time under the regulations. If a faction fails to notify its nominees in time, the committee is formed without it. A committee sits validly whenever the secretary is present, but counting needs representatives of at least two factions besides the secretary. A list with no seat on a given committee may send one observer, who may write factual remarks into the protocol and (under the regulations) check the booth for a sufficient stock of ballot slips. The protocol is signed by two members, one of them the chair or deputy, and by the secretary.
findings.quant: Composition deadline: 17 Sep 2026 (D-40, passed). 1 observer per unrepresented list per station. About 11,700 regular stations in 2022.
findings.authors: Knesset (statute); Aridor Hershkovitz & Shwartz Altshuler (on observer booth checks)
findings.title: Knesset Elections Law ss. 21, 24, 79; Privacy and Elections: Toward the 2026 Elections
findings.venue: Hebrew Wikisource consolidation; Israel Democracy Institute
findings.relevance: Seats on committees go to factions of the outgoing Knesset (Yesh Atid, YB, Labor). A new list without a faction, which may include Yashar, gets observers only. So the bloc needs one combined staffing plan: faction members where allied factions hold seats, Yashar or Democrats observers where they do not, with the stations where no allied faction sits as the top priority. Unfilled seats are lost by default (s. 21(d)).

findings.topic: CEC staffing: secretaries, cameras and paid roles
findings.claim: The State Comptroller's 2025 audit describes a CEC apparatus of tens of thousands of election-week workers alongside tens of thousands of faction representatives serving as polling-committee members. For the 2022 election the CEC put a second secretary in every station (about NIS 39m) and an election-integrity inspector carrying a body camera (about NIS 31m). It raised secretary pay between the 2021 and 2022 elections. Secretaries must be non-partisan, with no party membership or activity in the previous three years.
findings.quant: Secretary pay NIS 2,279 (2021) to NIS 2,868 (2022); 2026 recruitment advertised NIS 3,000 gross minus 18% special tax. Regular stations about 10,500 (Apr 2019) to about 11,700 (2022); eligible voters 6.34m to 6.79m.
findings.authors: State Comptroller of Israel; Kipa News (2026 pay)
findings.title: Aspects of human-capital management at the Central Elections Committee (Annual Report 75C); '3,000 shekels per workday' (Kipa)
findings.relevance: Integrity is guarded mainly by the state's own staff: two neutral secretaries plus inspectors with cameras. A party's members and observers add value in accurate counting, protocol objections and slip stock, not by policing large-scale fraud. Campaign volunteers who did party activity in the last three years cannot take the paid secretary roles.

findings.topic: How much the CEC integrity apparatus finds (24th Knesset audit)
findings.claim: The Comptroller's audit of integrity supervision in the March 2021 election found the inspector corps had grown fourfold and its cost threefold since 2019. Yet 18% of stations the CEC itself classed as 'sensitive' had no inspector. Only 56 of 799 flagged stations needed in-depth examination, and the CEC sent video to the police from 10 stations. Data on how suspicions were handled were missing for about 40% of closed reports, so the apparatus's effect could not be measured.
findings.quant: Cost NIS 17m (2019s) to NIS 51m (2021); 15,500 body cameras bought (NIS 19.3m); 18% of sensitive stations without an inspector; 7% (56/799) needed in-depth examination; police video referrals from 10 stations = 0.08% of about 13,240; 34% of inspectors could not use the reporting app.
findings.authors: State Comptroller of Israel
findings.title: Supervision over Purity of Elections in the 24th Knesset Elections
findings.relevance: Proven fraud in Israeli elections is rare and confined to a few stations. A vote-protection effort is therefore about accurate counts and fast, documented objections at the margin, not about deterring systematic fraud. The bloc's observers should be briefed to file factual remarks in the protocol, because that record is what the CEC acts on.

findings.topic: Count corrections and annulled stations have moved seats
findings.claim: In April 2019 the final count, after corrections and the double-envelope votes, moved a seat from Likud (to 35) to UTJ (to 8), which had been 'several hundred ballots shy'. The CEC checked counts at dozens of stations New Right challenged and found no substantial errors; New Right stayed out. In September 2019 the CEC annulled all votes at six stations (three in Yarka, one each in Sakhnin, Shfaram and Arraba), partly annulled others, citing 'real evidence of apparent vote tampering'. That moved a seat from UTJ to Likud, and the CEC chair said he would ask the Attorney General to consider seeking a court-ordered revote at those stations.
findings.quant: Apr 2019: one seat moved on a margin of a few hundred votes. Sep 2019: 6 stations fully annulled (plus partial annulments in Yarka and Sakhnin); one seat moved. 2022: Meretz missed the threshold by 4,061 votes.
findings.authors: Raoul Wootliff; Times of Israel staff
findings.title: Final vote count bumps UTJ up to 8 seats, Likud down to 35; New Right still out; Likud wins extra seat at expense of UTJ as election panel adjusts results
findings.relevance: With Ra'am and RZP-Zehut each at a pass probability of .78 and several seats decided by last-seat remainders, a few hundred votes can change P(change-led government). Change lists need a results desk on 27-29 Oct that reconciles every station protocol against CEC figures and files objections on anomalies before results are certified.

findings.topic: Invalid votes: national series
findings.claim: About 0.5-0.7% of ballots are invalid in Knesset elections. A ballot is invalid if it is not in the prescribed form or the envelope was not issued by the committee, if it carries a mark that could identify the voter, or if it contains slips for different lists. Up to three identical slips in one envelope count once. Invalid ballots are not attributed to any list, so the CEC does not publish invalid votes by party.
findings.authors: Central Elections Committee (official results); Knesset (statute)
findings.title: Official results of the elections to the 21st-25th Knesset; Knesset Elections Law s. 78
findings.venue: CEC results files (expc/expb); Hebrew Wikisource consolidation
findings.relevance: In 2022 the invalid pool (29,851) was more than seven times Meretz's 4,061-vote shortfall. Ballot-mechanics reminders (one slip, unmarked, in the envelope; one slip per envelope) in final-week contacts are cheap insurance for threshold-adjacent allies.

findings.topic: Invalid votes by sector (own analysis of CEC polling-station data)
findings.claim: Using the CEC's 2022 station file and the atlas segments, invalid rates vary about fivefold across segments. They are lowest in religious-Zionist, moshav, kibbutz and secular-liberal urban areas and highest in Druze, mixed-city, Arab and Russian-speaking areas. Double-envelope votes are invalid more often than regular-station votes. The Arab/Jewish gap has persisted since 2019. The number of high-invalid stations has fallen.
findings.quant: 2022 invalid rate: regular stations 0.59% (25,758/4,331,786); double envelopes 0.88% (4,093/462,807). By segment: religious-Zionist 0.22%, moshav 0.29%, kibbutz 0.31%, liberal urban 0.35%, mixed urban 0.50%, Jerusalem 0.56%, periphery-Likud 0.67%, Haredi 0.74%, Russian-speaking 0.80%, Negev Bedouin 0.94%, Galilee/Triangle 0.98%, mixed cities 1.07%, Druze 1.13%. Jewish non-Haredi localities 0.45-0.60% (2019-2022) vs Arab 0.57-1.13%. Stations with 3% or more invalid: 241 (Apr 2019), 114, 42, 150, 86 (2022).
findings.authors: The Knesset Model (own computation from CEC station results)
findings.title: Invalid-ballot rates by segment, 21st-25th Knesset
findings.venue: CEC polling-station files expb_21-25; atlas segment map
findings.relevance: YB's Russian-speaking base loses about 0.45 pp more ballots than the liberal-urban base, roughly 1,550 votes at 2022 turnout. A Russian-language 'how to vote' card and volunteer reminders for elderly FSU voters are low-cost. Soldiers and others voting by double envelope also need ballot-mechanics reminders.

findings.topic: Voter register: legal use and the PPA's 2026 requirements
findings.claim: Before an election the Interior Ministry gives parties the register (name, parent's name, address, ID number and assigned polling place) on a signed undertaking to use it only for the election and voter contact and never to pass it on. Misuse is a crime (2 years). The Privacy Protection Authority's guidelines for the 26th Knesset treat any database built on the register as at least 'medium' security. They require access limited to need, two-factor authentication, access logs, training, and detailed contracts with vendors, who carry independent liability as 'holders'. The register must be deleted from all systems, including vendors', after the election with written confirmation, and the rules extend to AI that infers voters' views or turnout likelihood.
findings.quant: Register misuse: up to 2 years (s. 118a). Privacy violation: up to 5 years (as summarised by counsel).
findings.authors: Knesset (statute); Lior Etgar (Bizportal/Takdin) summarising PPA guidelines
findings.title: Knesset Elections Law ss. 39, 118a; 'Elections 2026 are a test of the Privacy Protection Authority's new powers'
findings.relevance: Every change list's data stack (CRM, dialer, SMS vendor, canvassing app) needs a vendor agreement, access log and deletion plan now. Volunteer phone banks should work from scrubbed call lists, not exports of the register. Cross-ref D6-F24.

findings.topic: Privacy Protection Law Amendment 13: fines and the election-period pause
findings.claim: Amendment 13, in force since August 2025, lets the PPA impose administrative fines computed per data subject, alongside its other enforcement tools. It also created a special rule for election periods (from the Party Financing Law 'determining day' until results are published): the PPA may not use several inspection and enforcement powers against a party-controlled database without approval from the CEC chair. The powers are paused, not waived, and sanctions can follow after the vote.
findings.quant: Examples from the fine schedule: failing to notify a database NIS 150,000 (doubled where the database covers 1 million people or more); no security officer, no privacy officer, or a group data request without notice NIS 2 per person (NIS 4 for specially sensitive data such as political views); processing beyond authorisation or for a foreign purpose NIS 4-8 per person; direct mail without the required notice NIS 50 per person contacted (NIS 100 for sensitive data). By comparison, the 2020 Elector fines were in the tens of thousands of shekels.
findings.authors: Rachel Aridor Hershkovitz; Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler
findings.title: Privacy and Elections: Toward the 2026 Elections (The Algorithmic Campaign: Voter Privacy and the 2026 Israeli Elections), Policy Paper 64
findings.relevance: Because fines scale with the number of records, a careless list holding the 6.8m-record register faces exposure in the millions after the election. The pause means no regulator will stop a breach in real time, so the change bloc's leverage against opponents' misuse is a CEC chair petition or High Court petition, not the PPA.

findings.topic: Elector (2020) aftermath and data enrichment
findings.claim: In January 2021 the PPA found that Likud, Yisrael Beytenu and the app vendor Elector had breached the Privacy Protection Law and its data-security regulations. It said it intended to fine only Elector, about 11 months after the leak, because it lacked power to fine for most breaches. A July 2022 State Comptroller party-finance publication found that six factions had enriched register data through commercial firms without checking that the data were lawfully obtained. Likud trainers were reported in 2022 promising volunteers the phone numbers of supporters who had not voted.
findings.quant: Leak (Feb 2020): about 6.5m voters' records. Six factions used commercial enrichment (Comptroller, Jul 2022).
findings.authors: Rachel Aridor Hershkovitz; Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler (citing PPA breach determinations of 27 Jan 2021 and the State Comptroller)
findings.title: Privacy and Elections: Toward the 2026 Elections
findings.relevance: Buying 'enriched' phone lists from data brokers is the most likely way a change list breaks the law in the final fortnight. Use phones that supporters gave the campaign themselves, or vendor data with documented consent. Cross-ref D6-F24, D5-F25.

findings.topic: Targeted SMS and messaging count as 'direct mail'
findings.claim: The PPA's position (as set out by IDI) is that messages from parties, lists or candidates segmented by a personal characteristic are 'direct mail' under the Privacy Protection Law, whatever the channel: SMS, social media or messaging apps. Each message must say it is direct mail, identify the database controller and the source of the data, and tell the recipient of the right to be deleted, which the party must honour. Unlike the anti-spam provision of the Communications Law (s. 30a), these rules cover political propaganda.
findings.quant: Amendment 13 fine for direct mail without the required notice: NIS 50 per person contacted (NIS 100 for sensitive data).
findings.authors: Rachel Aridor Hershkovitz; Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler (citing PPA guidance)
findings.title: Privacy and Elections: Toward the 2026 Elections
findings.relevance: The final-week SMS and WhatsApp GOTV programmes (D3-F08, D3-F09) need a compliant footer (direct-mail notice, sender, data source, opt-out) and a working deletion process. Relational texting from volunteers' own contacts (D3-F12) is the lower-risk format.

findings.topic: Field offices: a small, local vote-share effect
findings.claim: County-level studies of US presidential campaigns find that a field office raised the campaign's vote share in its county by a fraction of a point to about a point. Effects shrank from 2008 to 2012, and the Republican offices showed none. Offices matter because they organise contacts, not because they exist.
findings.quant: Obama 2008: about +0.6 pp two-party vote in counties with an office (Masket 2009, as summarised by the author); 2012: about +0.3 pp (Masket, Sides & Vavreck 2016); McCain and Romney offices: no significant effect. Darr & Levendusky: about +1 pp (P-F22).
findings.authors: Seth E. Masket; Seth Masket, John Sides & Lynn Vavreck
findings.title: Did Obama's Ground Game Matter? The Influence of Local Field Offices During the 2008 Presidential Election; The Ground Game in the 2012 Presidential Election
findings.relevance: Under national PR with 14 days left, opening new offices buys little. Turn existing branches, activists' homes and coffee shops in the Turnout-engine cities (Tel Aviv, Haifa, Ramat Gan, Rishon, Herzliya) into staging points for contacts. Cross-ref P-F22.

findings.topic: Distributed volunteer leadership (Obama 2008 model)
findings.claim: McKenna and Han document how the 2008 Obama campaign built neighbourhood teams with volunteer leaders who owned a turf, its targets and its own recruiting. They argue this 'distributed leadership' let the campaign scale to millions of volunteers. Han's companion study of civic associations finds that the organisations producing the most activists combine 'transactional mobilising' with 'transformational organising', which builds members' skills and commitment.
findings.quant: Book subtitle: 'How Obama's 2.2 Million Volunteers Transformed Campaigning in America'. Descriptive and case-based, with no causal effect size.
findings.authors: Elizabeth McKenna; Hahrie Han / Hahrie Han
findings.title: Groundbreakers: How Obama's 2.2 Million Volunteers Transformed Campaigning in America; How Organizations Develop Activists: Civic Associations and Leadership in the 21st Century
findings.relevance: For the last 14 days: appoint one volunteer team leader per priority station cluster, give each a fixed list and a numeric target, and let them recruit their own shift volunteers. The same structure staffs election-day observer and ride teams.

findings.topic: Relational asks raise volunteer action (field experiments)
findings.claim: Three field experiments with US civic organisations showed that a relational context, meaning messages that reference members' own goals or status and follow-up conversations, made people more likely to sign petitions, recruit others and attend meetings than standard transactional asks.
findings.quant: As summarised by the Commons Library: personalised-goal message about 3x petition signing; new-member framing about 3x recruiting; meeting attendance 42% after a debrief call vs 12.5% after a regular call. Sample sizes and CIs are in the article.
findings.authors: Hahrie Han
findings.title: The Organizational Roots of Political Activism: Field Experiments on Creating a Relational Context
findings.relevance: Volunteer retention is the binding constraint on an election-day operation. A 5-minute debrief call after each volunteer's first shift, from a named team leader, is the most evidence-backed way to keep them through 27 Oct.

findings.topic: Volunteers are unrepresentative messengers
findings.claim: A survey of the 2012 Obama campaign's field workers, fielded with the campaign, found that the people contacting swing voters were demographically unrepresentative and ideologically extreme. They cared about atypical issues and misjudged voters' priorities. The campaign found little evidence it could control this through standard management tools.
findings.quant: Qualitative and descriptive (survey of campaign workers); see the article for distributions.
findings.authors: Ryan D. Enos; Eitan D. Hersh
findings.title: Party Activists as Campaign Advertisers: The Ground Campaign as a Principal-Agent Problem
findings.relevance: Change-bloc activists are disproportionately secular, educated and drawn from the protest movement. Send them to turn out identified supporters. Persuasion contacts with soft Netanyahu-bloc voters in Petah Tikva or the periphery (P-F13, D5-F12) should go to local, traditional or reservist messengers using tight scripts.

findings.topic: Clever framing from small studies often fails at scale
findings.claim: A widely cited small-sample result, that asking people to 'be a voter' (noun) rather than 'to vote' (verb) sharply raises turnout, was retested in a large field experiment. It had no effect on turnout, and both wordings did worse than a standard GOTV message.
findings.quant: Null effect of the noun-vs-verb wording in a large-scale field experiment; both below a standard mobilisation message.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Gregory A. Huber; Daniel R. Biggers; David J. Hendry
findings.title: A field experiment shows that subtle linguistic cues might not affect voter behavior
findings.relevance: Final-week scripts should use proven formats (plain reminders, vote plans, D3-F14) and not untested psychological tricks. Where volume allows (SMS, digital), A/B-test variants with a holdout instead of trusting creative intuition. Cross-ref P-F05 (Hewitt et al.: ad effects vary about 50% around the mean; 10-13% of the media budget on testing).

findings.topic: Data and analytics: what predictive scores can and cannot do
findings.claim: Campaigns combine the voter file, consumer data and survey responses into predictive 'scores' for turnout, support and responsiveness. These scores are useful for deciding whom to contact. Persuadability can only be estimated reliably from randomised experiments, because observational models confuse who supports a party with who can be moved.
findings.quant: Review article, no single effect size. Cross-ref P-F05 (146 experiments: SD of true ad effects about 0.5x the mean).
findings.authors: David W. Nickerson; Todd Rogers
findings.title: Political Campaigns and Big Data
findings.relevance: Israeli parties may legally model on the register, but enriching it with brokered data is risky (D12-F23). The atlas's station-level openness index and the exchange-rate model are the bloc's lawful 'scores'. Persuasion targeting should be validated with any holdout the field programme can afford, even a few hundred randomised households.

findings.topic: Large digital ad programmes barely move turnout
findings.claim: A randomised test of an $8.9 million, eight-month Facebook/Instagram persuasion programme aimed at about 2 million persuadable voters in five 2020 battleground states found no average effect on turnout. Effects split by partisanship: slightly up among Biden-leaners, slightly down among Trump-leaners.
findings.quant: Average turnout effect: none detectable. Biden-leaners +0.4 pp (s.e. 0.2); Trump-leaners -0.3 pp (s.e. 0.3); difference 0.7 pp (p = 0.036).
findings.authors: Minali Aggarwal; Jennifer Allen; Alexander Coppock; Dan Frankowski; Solomon Messing; Kelly Zhang; James Barnes; Andrew Beasley; Harry Hantman; Sylvan Zheng
findings.title: A 2 million-person, campaign-wide field experiment shows how digital advertising affects voter turnout
findings.relevance: In the final two weeks, digital money is better spent driving identified supporters to vote plans and to volunteer sign-ups than on broad persuasion ads. If ads are bought, geo-randomise a holdout to measure them (cross-ref P-F04, D3-F11).

findings.topic: Observers reduce election-day fraud where they are present (Armenia natural experiment)
findings.claim: In Armenia's 2003 presidential election, international observers were assigned to polling stations in a way that was close to random with respect to the incumbent's strength. The incumbent's vote share was lower at observed stations, showing that observers reduce election-day fraud at the stations they visit, though they do not eliminate it.
findings.quant: About 6 points lower incumbent share at observed stations in round 1, smaller in round 2 (from secondary summaries; not checked against the article's tables). Replication data cover 1,763 polling stations.
findings.authors: Susan D. Hyde
findings.title: The Observer Effect in International Politics: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
findings.relevance: This is evidence from a high-fraud setting. In Israel, where proven fraud is rare (D12-F17), the transferable lesson is that a party's presence in the room matters most where no allied faction holds a committee seat.

findings.topic: Randomised observers in Moscow: size of the fraud they prevent
findings.claim: Independent observers were randomly assigned to 156 of 3,164 Moscow polling stations in the 2011 Duma election. United Russia's share was 10.8 points lower and turnout 6.5 points lower at observed stations, while every opposition party gained. The authors put United Russia's true Moscow share at about 36% or less, against 47% officially.
findings.quant: United Russia -10.8 pp; turnout -6.5 pp; Just Russia +2.2, LDPR +1.7, Communists +2.9, Yabloko +3.5 pp.
findings.authors: Ruben Enikolopov; Vasily Korovkin; Maria Petrova; Konstantin Sonin; Alexei Zakharov
findings.title: Field experiment estimate of electoral fraud in Russian parliamentary elections
findings.relevance: An upper bound on what observers can do; Israeli effects will be orders of magnitude smaller. The turnout signal is the useful part: unusually high station turnout alongside an unusual list share is the pattern observers and the results desk should flag (in 2022 only 6 stations had turnout of 90% or more).

findings.topic: Announcing that counts will be photographed cuts aggregation fraud
findings.claim: In Afghanistan's 2010 parliamentary election, letters telling polling-centre managers that results sheets would be photographed and checked against official tallies cut theft and damage of election materials and reduced votes for candidates with connections to election officials. The study separately documents fraud in the aggregation of results in favour of connected candidates.
findings.quant: Theft of materials down about 60%; votes for connected candidates down about 25%.
findings.authors: Michael Callen; James D. Long
findings.title: Institutional Corruption and Election Fraud: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Afghanistan
findings.relevance: The Israeli analogue is cheap: observers and committee members photograph the signed station protocol, as far as CEC rules allow (check with counsel), and send it to a central desk that matches it to the CEC's published station results within 24-48 hours. This catches errors in tallying and transmission, the main source of the 2019 seat shifts (D12-F18).

findings.topic: Observers displace manipulation to unobserved stations
findings.claim: Randomised domestic observers in Ghana reduced fraud and violence at the stations they monitored. In areas dominated by one party, however, activists moved fraud to unobserved stations, and in competitive areas they moved violence there. An earlier Ghanaian experiment at voter-registration centres likewise found that observers' effects spilled over to nearby centres.
findings.quant: Direction only (effect sizes in the articles): reductions at observed stations, displacement to nearby unobserved stations.
findings.authors: Joseph Asunka; Sarah Brierley; Miriam Golden; Eric Kramon; George Ofosu / Nahomi Ichino; Matthias Schündeln
findings.title: Electoral Fraud or Violence: The Effect of Observers on Party Manipulation Strategies; Deterring or Displacing Electoral Irregularities? Spillover Effects of Observers in a Randomized Field Experiment in Ghana
findings.venue: British Journal of Political Science 49(1):129-151; Journal of Politics 74(1):292-307
findings.relevance: Partial coverage moves problems rather than removing them. The bloc's observers should cover whole multi-station sites (all stations at a school) in single-bloc-dominated localities rather than scattered single stations, and the CEC's 'sensitive station' inspectors (18% missing in 2021) are the main backstop.

open_questions: Does Yashar (and Bennett 2026 within Together) hold any polling-committee seats through an outgoing-Knesset faction, or only observer rights? How many of about 11,700 regular stations have no change-bloc faction member, and which allied faction can fill them?

What deadlines do the CEC regulations set for faction notices of committee members and replacements, and for observer nominations, for 27 Oct 2026? The statute leaves both to regulations (s. 21(d)-(f)).
May observers and committee members photograph the signed station protocol under 2026 CEC instructions? The protocol-photo results desk (D12-F34) depends on it.

Does a joint 'vote change' ad or shared field infrastructure paid by one list count as a prohibited in-kind donation to the others? This needs an election-counsel opinion and, ideally, a Comptroller pre-ruling.
Did Reservists-Economic, Amcha or Blue and White draw financing advances with bank guarantees? Their exposure determines how much a withdrawal or rescue deal costs them.
How many stations were annulled or corrected after the 2021 and 2022 elections? The CEC final reports were not retrieved, and there is no public data on invalid ballots by party.
Exact effect sizes in Hyde (2007) and Ichino & Schündeln (2012) were not verified against the articles' tables.
Will the CEC chair approve any PPA enforcement against party databases during the election period (Amendment 13 pause), and has any party been sanctioned under Amendment 13 yet?
